orbit: The closed path a body follows around another under gravity — an ellipse in the simplest case.
trajectory: The path a spacecraft follows through space, open or closed — for example the arc from Earth to Mars.
inclination: The tilt of an orbit's plane against a reference plane, such as Earth's equator or the ecliptic, in degrees.
rendezvous: Bringing two spacecraft to the same place at the same speed so that they fly together — usually the step before docking.
docking: Joining two spacecraft mechanically so that crew or cargo can pass between them.
gravity assist: Using a close pass of a planet to change a spacecraft's speed and direction without spending propellant.
delta-v: Change in velocity, written Δv: how much a spacecraft can change its motion, the currency of every mission plan, in km/s.
apogee: The point of an orbit around Earth that is farthest from Earth.
perigee: The point of an orbit around Earth that is closest to Earth.
burn: A period of firing a rocket engine to change a spacecraft's velocity.
stage: A section of a rocket with its own engines and propellant, dropped when its propellant is used up.
propellant: What a rocket engine uses up to make thrust: usually a fuel and an oxidizer together.
payload: What a rocket carries for the mission: satellites, a crewed spacecraft, cargo or instruments.
thrust: The force a rocket engine produces to push the vehicle forward, measured in newtons.
booster: A rocket that provides thrust at launch: a first stage, or a strap-on rocket at the side of the core.
specific impulse: How efficiently an engine uses its propellant, in seconds: the higher it is, the more Δv from the same propellant.
flyby: A close pass by a planet, moon or other body without going into orbit around it or landing.
orbit insertion: The engine burn that slows a spacecraft enough to be captured into orbit around its destination.
entry: A spacecraft's passage into a planet's atmosphere, where drag and heating slow it down.
descent: The way down to a surface, from orbit or from the atmosphere to touchdown.
orbiter: A spacecraft that goes into orbit around a planet, moon or other body to study it from above, often for years.
lander: A spacecraft that sets down on the surface of a planet, moon or small body and works where it lands.
rover: A vehicle that drives across the surface of another world, carrying its instruments from place to place.
capsule: The part of a spacecraft that brings the crew or the cargo home through the atmosphere, protected by a heat shield.
upper stage: The top stage of a rocket, which finishes the climb to orbit or sends the payload on towards its destination.
heat shield: The layer that protects a spacecraft from the heat of atmospheric entry, usually by charring and wearing away.
airlock: A small chamber between a spacecraft's pressurised cabin and the vacuum outside, emptied and refilled with air so that crews can go out and come back in.
spacewalk: Work done by an astronaut outside a spacecraft, in a spacesuit; also called EVA (extravehicular activity).
splashdown: The end of a flight home in which a capsule comes down in the sea under parachutes and is picked up by a recovery ship.
sample return: Collecting material on another world and bringing it back to Earth, where laboratories can study it far more closely than any instrument sent there.
regolith: The layer of loose, broken rock and dust that covers the Moon, Mars and asteroids, ground up by billions of years of impacts.
microgravity: The near-weightless state of everything in orbit, which is falling around the Earth together with its spacecraft.
life support: The systems that keep a crew alive: breathable air, water, the right temperature and the removal of carbon dioxide and waste.
solar array: The panels of solar cells that turn sunlight into electricity for a spacecraft or a station.
low Earth orbit: An orbit from about 160 to 2,000 km above the Earth, where the ISS and most satellites fly, circling the planet in about 90 minutes.
geostationary: The circular orbit 35,786 km above the equator in which a satellite goes round once a day and so stays over the same spot on the ground.
polar orbit: An orbit that passes over or near both poles, so the ground turns beneath it and the spacecraft sees the whole surface in time.
perihelion: The point of an orbit around the Sun that is closest to the Sun.
aphelion: The point of an orbit around the Sun that is farthest from the Sun.
eccentricity: How stretched an orbit is: 0 is a circle, values between 0 and 1 are ever longer ellipses, 1 and above are open paths that never return.
launch window: The period in which a launch can reach its target with the propellant on board, set by where the Earth and the target are.
escape velocity: The speed an object needs to leave a body for good without further thrust: about 11.2 km/s from the Earth's surface.
Hohmann transfer: The cheapest way between two circular orbits: one burn onto half an ellipse that touches both, and a second burn to circularise at the far end.
Lagrange point: One of five points where the pull of two large bodies and the motion of orbit balance, so a small object can keep its place relative to both.
C3: Characteristic energy: the square of the speed left over once a spacecraft has escaped the Earth, in km²/s² — the figure a launcher must reach for a given trip.
rocket equation: Tsiolkovsky's equation, Δv = vₑ · ln(m₀/m₁): the change in speed a rocket can make from its exhaust velocity and how much of its mass is propellant.
free-return: A path to the Moon that swings round its far side and falls back to Earth with no further burn, so a crew can come home even if the engine fails.
sun-synchronous: A near-polar orbit whose plane turns with the Earth's yearly path, so the satellite crosses each latitude at the same local solar time every day.
halo orbit: A looping orbit around a Lagrange point, held there by the balance of two bodies' gravity — JWST circles one at L2, Gateway was planned for another.
exoplanet: A planet that orbits a star other than the Sun; more than 5,000 are known, most found by the dip in light as they cross their star.
light-year: The distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km — a measure of distance, not of time.
habitable zone: The range of distances from a star where a planet could keep liquid water on its surface: not too hot, not too cold.
asteroid belt: The wide ring of rocky and metallic bodies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, so thinly spread that spacecraft cross it without trouble.
solar wind: The stream of charged particles that flows out from the Sun in every direction at hundreds of kilometres per second.
magnetosphere: The region around a planet ruled by its magnetic field, which turns the solar wind aside and traps charged particles in belts.
observatory: A place on the ground where telescopes and antennas watch the sky — optical domes, radio dishes, deep-space antennas.
